results.result: Allogeneic ChR2+ motor neurons can successfully reinnervate target muscles in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS when combined with H57-597 mAb immunosuppression. Engrafted motor neurons were present in all treated animals (n>84), with significant axonal projection and robust muscle fiber reinnervation observed even at late-stage disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C40, C41, C54, and C56 collectively demonstrate successful muscle reinnervation in the aggressive SOD1G93A ALS model. The data show 100% graft survival with H57-597 treatment (C40), robust axonal projection and reinnervation (C41), and maintenance of innervation until late-stage disease (C54, C56). Histological evidence (Figures 4A-D) and physiological responses (C44) provide strong converging support.

results.result: Daily optical stimulation training (OST) dramatically enhances muscle force generation and prevents atrophy. OST resulted in a 9.4-fold increase in maximal tetanic force (7.5±0.94 g vs 0.8±0.2 g; p≤0.000001) and enabled ONS to elicit 22.7% of total residual muscle capacity compared to only 1.46% in untrained mice, representing a >13-fold improvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C49, C50, C5, C6, C55, and C83 are strongly supported by physiological data (Figure 5C-I) showing highly significant improvements in force generation with OST. The statistical significance (p≤0.000001) and large effect sizes (9.4-fold and >13-fold improvements) provide robust evidence. The dCALMS analysis (C52, C53) further confirms prevention of muscle atrophy in reinnervated fibers.

results.result: Optical stimulation training prevents atrophy of reinnervated muscle fibers. Muscle fibers innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons had similar cross-sectional area (CSA) to those innervated by endogenous motor neurons (922.3 vs 1018.3 μm²; p=0.85) and significantly larger CSA than denervated fibers (525.4 μm²; p≤0.00001).
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C53, and C82 are supported by the novel dCALMS analysis (C81) shown in Figure 6D. The data demonstrate that reinnervated fibers maintain size comparable to healthy innervated fibers and are significantly larger than denervated fibers, with appropriate statistical testing. This provides direct evidence that OST prevents muscle atrophy.

results.result: Without immunosuppression, allogeneic ChR2+ motor neuron grafts show poor long-term survival (<5% at 35 days) due to host-vs-graft rejection rather than disease-related toxicity. However, rare surviving grafts demonstrated robust reinnervation capacity and functional muscle contraction, indicating that the ALS muscle environment remains receptive to reinnervation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30, C72, C73, and C76 are supported by experimental observations showing low graft survival without immunosuppression but successful reinnervation in rare surviving cases (Figure 1). The inference that rejection rather than toxicity causes graft loss (C30, C76) is supported by the observation that grafts survive up to 14 days (C72) and that immunosuppression enables complete survival (C31, C76).

results.result: FK506 immunosuppression enables graft survival but causes severe adverse effects including complete prevention of muscle reinnervation, intraneural tumor formation, body mass decline in 44.4% of SOD1G93A mice, and significant axon loss in peripheral nerves. These effects are specific to FK506 and not observed with H57-597 mAb treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are well-supported by experimental data showing FK506 enabled graft survival (C31) but prevented reinnervation (C32, Figure 2B), caused tumors (C33, Figure 2C), induced body mass decline (C34, Figure 2E), and caused peripheral neuropathy (C35, Figure 3). The specificity to FK506 is demonstrated by comparison with H57-597 treatment (C36, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Motor neuron subtype identity (fast-firing vs slow-firing) does not significantly affect the amplitude of muscle response to optical stimulation or the ability to innervate mixed fiber-type muscles in SOD1G93A mice. This suggests a single motor neuron type could be used to target multiple different muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C57, and C58 are supported by physiological data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) showing no significant difference between fast-firing and slow-firing motor neurons in force generation. The inference that motor neuron subtype is redundant (C57) and that a single type could be used universally (C58) is reasonable based on this data, though C58 remains somewhat speculative regarding clinical application.

results.result: Without optical stimulation training, only 10.5% of endplates are innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons, and contractile responses are extremely weak (0.8±0.2 g), precluding motor unit analysis in most mice. OST significantly increases innervation and enables clear separation of individual motor unit values.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, C78, and C79 are supported by quantitative endplate analysis (Figure 4E) and physiological recordings (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 5D). The data clearly show limited innervation and weak responses without training, with dramatic improvement after OST enabling motor unit analysis.

results.result: Repetitive optical nerve stimulation (ONS) does not induce rapid muscle fatigue, unlike electrical nerve stimulation (ENS), and OST does not alter contractile rate characteristics. This demonstrates a key advantage of optogenetic control over electrical stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51 and C77 are supported by fatigue trace recordings (Figure 5K) and contractile rate analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A-C). The data clearly show sustained force with ONS versus rapid fatigue with ENS, and no change in contractile kinetics with OST.

results.result: De novo neuromuscular junctions formed by engrafted motor neurons in SOD1G93A mice exhibit signs of immaturity, including poly-innervation and collateral/terminal sprouting of motor axons.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by histological data (Figure 4C, 4D) showing poly-innervation and axonal sprouting. This is consistent with previous findings in wild-type nerve ligation models (Bryson et al., 2014) and expected for newly formed NMJs.

results.result: H57-597 mAb treatment was well tolerated during transient administration from symptom-onset to late-stage disease in SOD1G93A mice, and immunosuppression per se is not an impediment to this cell therapy strategy based on prior clinical evidence.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by observations showing no adverse effects during the treatment period in the study. Claim C60 is supported by inference from cited clinical trials (C19, C20) showing ALS patients can tolerate immunosuppression. However, long-term effects in humans remain uncertain.

results.result: The donor ChR2+ motor neurons were derived from 129S1/SvImJ mESCs and recipient SOD1G93A mice were on a C57BL/6J background, constituting an allogeneic transplant model. Allogeneic cells provide a more cost-effective, off-the-shelf platform compared to autologous approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 are factual statements about the genetic backgrounds used, supported by the methods and Appendix 1—table 1. Claim C71 is a reasonable inference based on general knowledge of cell therapy manufacturing economics, though it remains somewhat speculative regarding actual cost-effectiveness.

results.result: A novel technique termed digital Cross-sectional area Analysis from Longitudinal Muscle Sections (dCALMS) was developed to assess muscle fiber innervation status and fiber diameter in situations where high-resolution 3D imaging of entire muscles is not feasible.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by the methodological description and application shown in Figure 6. The technique addresses a genuine technical limitation (C80) and provides quantitative data on muscle fiber CSA based on innervation status.

results.result: Background claims about ALS pathology, epidemiology, and current treatment limitations. NMJ breakdown is an early hallmark of ALS, median survival is 20-48 months, global mortality is ~30,000/year, 5-10% of cases are familial, over 20 monogenic mutations have been identified accounting for 45% of fALS and 7% of sALS, and no effective treatments exist to arrest progressive paralysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C7-C13 are background statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Fischer et al., 2004; Chiò et al., 2009; Mathis et al., 2019; Mejzini et al., 2019; Brown and Al-Chalabi, 2017). These represent well-established knowledge in the ALS field.

results.result: Prior cell therapy and gene therapy approaches for ALS have shown limited clinical benefit. ASOs show early promise but are unlikely to benefit most sporadic ALS patients. Intraspinal NSC grafts showed modest effects, intrathecal MSC delivery showed no benefit, but ALS patients can tolerate 6-month immunosuppression sufficient for long-term graft survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C20 are background statements about prior therapeutic approaches, supported by appropriate citations (Miller et al., 2013; Feldman et al., 2014; Goutman et al., 2018; Glass et al., 2012; Cudkowicz et al., 2022; Mazzini et al., 2015; Tadesse et al., 2014). These provide important context for the current study.

results.result: Prior work established the proof-of-concept for optogenetic motor neuron replacement therapy. Engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons can project axons to form de novo NMJs and be selectively activated by optical stimulation. A 64-channel device has been developed for multi-site control. ONS recruits motor units in physiological order, while ENS applied to the phrenic nerve accelerated diaphragm denervation in ALS patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 describe prior work and established principles, supported by appropriate citations (Bryson et al., 2014; Nagel et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2022; Llewellyn et al., 2010; McDermott et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Bermejo et al., 2016; Guimarães-Costa et al., 2019). These provide essential background for understanding the current study's rationale.

results.result: Various background claims about FK506 effects, H57-597 mAb efficacy, MMC treatment, activity-dependent processes, ALS pathology, muscle physiology, ENS risks, ONS advantages, and clinical immunosuppression approaches, all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C38, C39, C46, C47, C68, C74, C75, C84, C85, C86, C87, C88, C90, C91, C92, C93, and C94 are background statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide context and rationale for experimental design choices and interpretation.

results.result: Speculative claims about future clinical applications, including universal compatibility with all ALS patients, potential need for immunosuppression due to ChR2 immunogenicity, targeting multiple muscles, adaptation of existing devices, integration with BCI technology, applications beyond ALS, indefinite extension of muscle function, bypassing CNS damage, need for validation in other ALS models and larger animals, and potential for major health benefits.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67, C89, C95-C100 are speculative statements about future applications and requirements. While they are reasonable extrapolations from the current findings, they lack direct experimental support and represent hypotheses requiring future validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C96-C99) and remaining challenges (C98, C99).

results.result: The study demonstrates that an optogenetic neural replacement strategy using ChR2+ motor neurons with H57-597 mAb immunosuppression can effectively restore innervation of severely affected skeletal muscles in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS. Engrafted motor neurons were present in all treated mice (n>84), showed significant axonal projection and robust muscle fiber reinnervation, even when engrafted after symptom onset and maintained until late-stage disease.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states it is "convincing that embryonic stem cell derived motor neurons can be transplanted into and applied to reinnervate the muscles in an ALS mouse model." Reviewer 3 confirms "convincing evidence that optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing motor neurons implanted in muscles effectively restore innervation." Reviewer 2 acknowledges the manuscript "addresses some of the challenges that will need to be overcome, such as immune rejection of the allograft."

results.result: Daily optical stimulation training (OST) resulted in a 9.4-fold increase in maximal tetanic force compared to untrained mice, with trained mice achieving up to 22.7% of total residual muscle force (representing a >13-fold improvement). OST reinforced connectivity between engrafted motor neurons and muscle fibers and prevented atrophy of reinnervated muscle fibers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these quantitative findings about OST effects. Reviewer 3 explicitly states the data "supported by convincing data presented in the paper" regarding the method's ability to "selectively control the function of implicated muscles." The physiological improvements from training are accepted as demonstrated by the experimental data.

results.result: FK506 immunosuppression enabled graft survival at the graft site in all animals but caused three major problems: complete prevention of muscle fiber reinnervation, intraneural tumor formation in most mice, and body mass decline in 44.4% of SOD1G93A mice. FK506 also caused significant axon loss in tibial and common peroneal nerves in both wild-type and SOD1G93A mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about FK506's adverse effects. The data on FK506's problems are presented as factual observations that led to testing alternative immunosuppression approaches. These findings are implicitly accepted as they provide the rationale for the H57-597 mAb approach that reviewers explicitly support.

results.result: H57-597 mAb treatment does not significantly alter axon size distribution or counts compared to untreated SOD1G93A mice and was well tolerated during transient administration from symptom-onset to late-stage disease, avoiding the adverse effects observed with FK506.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the overall demonstration of successful immunosuppression strategy. Reviewer 2 notes the manuscript "addresses some of the challenges that will need to be overcome, such as immune rejection of the allograft," implicitly accepting the H57-597 solution. No concerns are raised about the safety or efficacy claims for this immunosuppressant.

results.result: Only 10.5% of endplates were innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons in untrained mice, but these reinnervated endplates were functional as acute optical nerve stimulation induced positive contractile responses in all late-stage SOD1G93A mice tested. Motor neuron subtype identity did not significantly affect the amplitude of muscle response to acute optical stimulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these quantitative findings about innervation levels and functional responses. The demonstration of functional reinnervation is central to the reviewers' positive assessment. Reviewer 3 confirms the evidence shows motor neurons "effectively restore innervation," which encompasses these functional measurements.

results.result: Repetitive optical nerve stimulation (ONS) pulses did not induce rapid muscle fatigue, whereas equivalent electrical nerve stimulation (ENS) pulses did result in rapid muscle fatigue.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this comparative finding about ONS versus ENS. This advantage of the optogenetic approach is implicitly accepted as part of the overall demonstration that the method can "selectively control the function of targeted muscles" (Reviewer 3), which includes avoiding fatigue.

results.result: The average cross-sectional area (CSA) of muscle fibers innervated by engrafted ChR2+ motor neurons was similar to fibers innervated by residual endogenous motor neurons (922.3 vs 1018.3 μm²) and significantly greater than denervated fibers (525.4 μm²), demonstrating prevention of atrophy in reinnervated fibers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these histological measurements supporting atrophy prevention. The dCALMS analysis data are presented as supporting evidence for the OST benefits, and reviewers accept the overall conclusion that the approach prevents muscle atrophy, as evidenced by their positive assessment of the therapeutic strategy.

results.result: Without immunosuppression, graft survival was extremely low (<5%) at 35 days post-engraftment in SOD1G93A mice. However, in rare surviving cases, robust intramuscular axon growth and partial NMJ reinnervation were observed, with optical stimulation inducing weak tetanic contractions. Poor survival was attributed to host-vs-graft rejection rather than disease-related toxicity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these initial findings that established the need for immunosuppression. These observations are accepted as the foundation for developing the immunosuppression strategy that reviewers explicitly support. The interpretation that rejection rather than toxicity caused graft loss is implicitly accepted through reviewers' endorsement of the immunosuppression solution.

results.result: Motor neuron subtype identity appears redundant for innervating mixed fiber type muscles in SOD1G93A mice, suggesting a single motor neuron type produced at scale could potentially target multiple different muscles in each patient.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question this finding or its translational implication. The observation that motor neuron subtype doesn't affect innervation success is accepted as part of the overall demonstration of the approach's feasibility and is consistent with reviewers' positive assessment of the therapeutic potential.

results.result: The authors propose that this combinatorial strategy (allogeneic cells, immunosuppression, optical stimulation) could be universally compatible with ALS patients, target multiple muscles independently, integrate with brain-computer interfaces to restore autologous movement control, and have broad utility for other neurogenic causes of paralysis including spinal cord injury and stroke.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the therapeutic potential but do not explicitly endorse these specific translational claims. Reviewer 1 states the work "will be of broad interest to researchers and medical biologists to develop new strategies," suggesting future development rather than confirmed applicability. Reviewer 2 notes "challenges that will need to be overcome," indicating uncertainty about clinical translation. These are speculative extrapolations from the mouse data that reviewers treat cautiously.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that further investigation is required to confirm the strategy in alternate ALS models with longer lifespans, that maintenance therapy may be needed for long-term graft survival, that demonstrating efficacy with human motor neurons is the biggest challenge, and that scaling up in larger animal models is necessary.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly support these acknowledgments of limitations. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes the manuscript addresses "challenges that will need to be overcome," aligning with the authors' recognition of remaining hurdles. These statements of future research needs are consistent with reviewers' cautious optimism about clinical translation.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on muscle reinnervation claims (C3, C4, C40, C41, C54, C56). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative aspects (100% graft survival, histological and physiological data), while peer reviewers focus on the overall demonstration that ESC-derived motor neurons can reinnervate muscles in ALS models.

Strong agreement on OST physiological benefits (C5, C6, C48, C49, C50, C55). Both find the force generation improvements well-supported. OpenEval includes additional claims (C83 on statistical significance, C52-C53 on atrophy prevention via dCALMS), while peer review focuses on the core OST effectiveness claims. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on FK506 adverse effects (C31, C32, C33, C34, C35). Both evaluations accept these findings as factual observations. OpenEval additionally addresses C36 (H57-597 specificity comparison), which peer reviewers implicitly accept but don't explicitly evaluate separately. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on atrophy prevention via dCALMS analysis (C52, C53). Both find the evidence supported. OpenEval additionally includes C82 (reinnervated fibers larger than denervated) and emphasizes the novel methodology. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of overall OST benefits without detailed methodological commentary.

Agreement on motor neuron subtype redundancy (C57, C58). Both evaluations support these claims, though OpenEval notes C58 is somewhat speculative regarding clinical application. OpenEval additionally addresses C45 (no significant difference in force generation between subtypes), which provides the empirical basis. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on initial graft rejection findings (C27, C28, C29, C30). Both accept these observations as establishing the need for immunosuppression. OpenEval includes additional claims (C72, C73, C76) providing mechanistic details about rejection timing and inference. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these through endorsement of the immunosuppression solution.

Agreement on UNCERTAIN status for translational claims (C61, C63, C64, C65, C66, C67, C89, C95). Both recognize these as speculative extrapolations requiring future validation. OpenEval includes additional speculative claims (C62, C100) and explicitly notes lack of direct experimental support. Peer reviewers express cautious optimism about clinical translation.

Agreement on ONS fatigue resistance advantage (C51). Both find this supported. OpenEval additionally addresses C77 (contractile kinetics unchanged) and provides more detailed reference to specific figure panels. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the optogenetic approach's advantages without separate detailed evaluation.

Partial overlap on innervation and functional response claims (C43, C44). Both find evidence supported. OpenEval additionally includes C78-C79 on training effects and motor unit analysis. Peer review R5 additionally addresses C45 (motor neuron subtype comparison), which OpenEval evaluates separately in R6. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Partial overlap on H57-597 safety (C59). Both support this claim. OpenEval additionally addresses C60 (ALS patient tolerance based on clinical trials), noting uncertainty about long-term human effects. Peer review R4 focuses more broadly on C36 (H57-597 efficacy) and accepts the immunosuppression strategy without detailed safety commentary.

Agreement on acknowledgment of limitations (C96, C97, C98, C99). Both evaluations support these statements recognizing remaining challenges. OpenEval rates the broader set of translational claims as UNCERTAIN, while peer review R11 specifically supports the authors' acknowledgment of limitations as appropriate and consistent with cautious optimism.

OpenEval finds poly-innervation and axonal sprouting (C42) supported by histological data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this finding is consistent with peer reviewers' overall acceptance of successful reinnervation.

OpenEval finds claims about genetic backgrounds (C69, C70) and cost-effectiveness inference (C71) supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These are methodological details and economic speculation not explicitly addressed by peer reviewers.

OpenEval finds the novel dCALMS methodology (C81) supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found. Peer reviewers accept the results from this method (R7) but don't separately evaluate the methodological innovation itself.

OpenEval finds background claims about ALS (C1, C2, C7-C13) supported by established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found. Peer reviewers don't separately evaluate background/contextual claims.
